_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Rav Sheshet says: actually the mitzva of redemption is immediate. And that which it teaches, “Valuations and a firstborn donkey do not apply to less than thirty [days],” means that one does not transgress over it until thirty days; from then on, one transgresses.
rashi:a2.1: What, does it not mean a mitzva to keep it [unredeemed]: in accordance with Rav Naḥman, and this is difficult for Rav Sheshet.
rashi:a2.2: A mitzva to redeem it: from immediately until thirty [days] is the time of redemption, and from then on one transgresses.
rashi:a3.1: Rather, Rava says: actually it is a mitzva to keep it [for thirty days], and even so I do not resolve it as Rav Naḥman did. And there is no difficulty: this [baraita], which teaches that for thirty days it is a mitzva to keep it,
rashi:a3.2: is Rabbi Eliezer, who compares: the firstborn of a non-kosher animal to the firstborn of a person.
rashi:a3.3: And that: which teaches “immediately,” is the Rabbis of our mishna, who do not compare.
rashi:a5.1: Mishna. The mitzva of designation: with a Hebrew maidservant, whom the master designates as a wife.
rashi:a5.2: Takes precedence over the mitzva of redemption: where she redeems herself.
rashi:a5.3: “Who has not designated her, then he shall let her be redeemed”: [implying that] if he designated her, that is better.
rashi:a6.1: Now the mitzva of ḥalitza takes precedence: for one who takes his yevama in levirate marriage not for the sake of the mitzva encounters the prohibition of a brother’s wife.
rashi:a7.1: With the owner: one who consecrates a non-kosher animal for the upkeep of the Temple: the mitzva of redeeming it falls on the owner before anyone else.
rashi:a8.1: We will return to you, HaLoke’aḥ Ubar Ḥamoro [the end of chapter 1].
rashi:a9.1: Mishna. One who purchases the fetus of his cow. [A heading only.]
rashi:a9.2: Even though he is not permitted: to sell an animal to a gentile.
rashi:a12.1: Gemara. In accordance with Rabbi Ḥanina: in the first chapter (above, Bekhorot 5b): “In what way are firstborn donkeys different from firstborn horses and camels,” etc.
rashi:a12.2: Because its matters are few: for the firstborn donkey is discussed only in the first chapter, while the whole rest of the tractate discusses the firstborn of a kosher animal.
rashi:a13.1: With regard to his animal: [that is,] his herd.
rashi:a13.2: According to their laws: we judge him according to their laws, and below it explains what that is.
rashi:a16.1: An ancestral possession is acquired with money, with a document and with taking possession: from when he treads on its boundaries, as we say in the first chapter of Kiddushin (26a).
rashi:a17.1: And his property by pulling: movable property is acquired only by pulling, [as stated] in tractate Kiddushin (26a).
rashi:a18.1: “Of your counterpart’s hand”: implies from hand to hand, which is pulling.
rashi:a19.1: Not at all: he does not acquire until it comes into the domain of the Jew.
rashi:a20.1: And say either this or that: and the verse would imply: from the hand of your counterpart it is by pulling and not by money, but from the hand of a gentile, by whichever [method] you wish. And we would learn from it that where he pulled and did not give money, he has also acquired.
rashi:a21.1: Just as your counterpart with one: pulling.
rashi:a21.2: So too a gentile with one: with money and not by pulling, for this is what it implies: your counterpart by pulling, and not a gentile.
rashi:a22.1: “From the money of his purchase”: the verse speaks of a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile.
rashi:b2.1: According to Ameimar, who says, etc.: in the last chapter of Avoda Zara (71b).
rashi:b2.2: This works out well if he holds in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan: who says in chapter HaZahav (Bava Metzia 46b) that by Torah law money acquires, as it is written, “Then he shall give the money and it shall be assured to him” (Leviticus 27:19), for an ordinary person is derived from consecrated property, and pulling does not acquire. [Then] one can say that “your counterpart” comes to say: from the hand of your counterpart with money, and from the hand of a gentile by pulling.
rashi:b3.1: Explicit in the Torah: “of your counterpart’s hand” implies from hand to hand.
rashi:b4.1: They said: to your counterpart: for it excludes a Canaanite [i.e., a gentile] from the law of exploitation, as written at the end of the verse, it excludes him.
rashi:b4.2: Exploitation is derived from “a man shall not exploit his brother”: which implies his brother, and not a Canaanite.
rashi:b5.1: One to exclude a Canaanite and one to exclude consecrated property: from [the law of] exploitation.
rashi:b6.1: According to the one who says his robbery: of a Canaanite is forbidden, in Bava Kamma, the last chapter, HaGozel (Bava Kamma 113b).
rashi:b6.2: They said: certainly, if he holds that robbing a Canaanite is permitted, the verse no longer comes to permit exploitation, but to exclude him from the law of acquisition. And since he says that a gentile acquires by pulling, perforce he holds in accordance with Rabbi Yoḥanan, that [the verse] excludes him from [acquiring with] money.
rashi:b7.2: He may return: for pulling does not acquire.
rashi:b7.3: To the Dead Sea: for an object of idol worship in the possession of a Jew can never have its status revoked.
rashi:b8.1: Why do I need pulling. [A heading only.]
rashi:b9.1: A mistaken transaction: for he did not know that there was an object of idol worship among them; therefore he can retract.
rashi:b9.2: In the first clause there is a mistaken transaction, and in the latter clause there is no mistaken transaction: [said] in astonishment.
rashi:b10.1: The first clause and the latter clause are a mistaken transaction: and by law he could retract in the latter clause too. But the Rabbis decreed [otherwise], since if he gave dinars and then takes them back, it looks as though he is selling an object of idol worship. In the first clause, where he did not give dinars, when he returns it he takes nothing back, so it does not look like idol worship in the possession of a Jew. And that is why it mentions the giving of money, even though [the gentile] accepted upon himself to be judged by Jewish law.
rashi:b11.1: For he did not know: that there was idol worship among them, since he had not given the dinars, such that we would say he should have inspected; for an ordinary merchant does not inspect until the time he gives the money.
rashi:b11.2: He should have inspected: and since he did not inspect, he waived [his claim], and his pulling is a complete pulling.
rashi:b12.1: Rav Ashi says: actually [the case is] where he did not accept upon himself to be judged by Jewish law, and the latter clause is not difficult for Rabbi Oshaya. And as for what you said, “If money acquires, why do I need pulling”: pulling is not meant precisely, for from the first clause, pulling does not acquire, as it teaches “he may return,” so in the latter clause too pulling does not acquire.
rashi:b13.1: Ravina says: from the latter clause, pulling acquires, etc.: and it is a case where he accepted upon himself to be judged by Jewish law. And this tanna holds that it was necessary to say that one need not keep his word with the gentile.
rashi:b14.1: For he holds that words involve a breach of faith: if he retracts from what he said.
tosafot:a6.1: The mitzva of ḥalitza takes precedence: what Rabbeinu Ḥananel explained is explained in chapter HaḤoletz (Yevamot 39b).
tosafot:a7.1: The mitzva of redemption takes precedence with the owner, as it is stated, “And if it is not redeemed”: In Arakhin, chapter HaMakdish Sadeihu (Arakhin 27a), it gives a different reason why the owners take precedence: because they add a fifth. And there it raises a difficulty against this and resolves it.
tosafot:a9.1: One who purchases. [A heading only, with no comment.]
tosafot:a13.1: He has acquired, and it is obligated in the firstborn: even though we already know that he has acquired, it needed to teach us that it is obligated in the firstborn, so that you should not say he acquired it only out of doubt or by rabbinic law. It teaches us that he acquires it with a complete acquisition.
tosafot:a16.1: Just as an ancestral possession is acquired with money, a document and taking possession: meaning, when one acquires it from a Jew; so too a Canaanite slave, when one acquires him from a Jew. But with a gentile it is not reasonable that a document should be effective, since acquisition by a document does not apply to a gentile, as we say in chapter Ḥezkat HaBatim (Bava Batra 54b): a gentile, once the money reaches his hand, has removed himself [from the property], and the Jew does not acquire until the document reaches his hand.
tosafot:a18.1: From the hand of your counterpart by pulling, so from the hand of a gentile with money: And if you say: perhaps [infer that] from the hand of a gentile it is with a document or by taking possession, for taking possession also applies to movable property, if he made some improvement in them, like locking, fencing or breaching [a wall] with land? One can say that these two acquisitions [money and pulling] are common, and they belong one to the seller and one to the buyer: this one gives money and that one draws the object to himself. And so too according to Rabbi Yoḥanan below, where we expound the opposite, “your counterpart” with money, so a gentile by pulling. And if you say: from where do we know that they count as an acquisition at all, such that we establish by reasoning that the acquisitions of the verse are these? One can say that we find money acquiring elsewhere, with land and with consecrated property, and pulling with a found object and with ownerless property.
tosafot:a22.1: (Above) If his person is acquired: if a gentile acquires the person of a Jew with money, etc. From the fact that it does not object here, “If so, even with a document and taking possession too,” as it objected above, there is a proof for the explanation of Rabbeinu Tam, who explains in the first chapter of Kiddushin (14b), “We have found a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile, whose entire acquisition is by money”: meaning, a gentile’s entire acquisition of a Hebrew slave is by money, as it is written, “From the money of his purchase” (Leviticus 25:51), and not by a document or taking possession, as is evident here. And Rashi explained there that [a gentile’s acquisition of] every item is by money, as we expound here: “of your counterpart” by pulling, so from a gentile with money. But this is difficult, for this derivation is according to Reish Lakish, and the halakha follows Rabbi Yoḥanan. And if you say: still, a gentile acquires a Jew by taking possession, as it says in Gittin (38a): “From where do we know that a gentile acquires a Jew by taking possession? As it is stated: ‘And took some of them captive’” (Numbers 21:1)? One can say that that taking possession is when there is war, and the same is true of his property, as it says in Ḥullin (60b): Ammon and Moab were purified through Siḥon.
tosafot:a24.1: Say: to a gentile, not at all. An a fortiori inference: if he acquires his person, is it not all the more so his property: And if you say: perhaps [he acquires] by exchange [ḥalifin], since he acquires his property [that way], as it expounds in Kiddushin (8a): “From the money of his purchase”: he is acquired with money, and he is not acquired by way of grain and vessels; and what are these? Exchange. And this verse is written about a Hebrew slave sold to a gentile, which implies that other things, such as movable property, a gentile acquires by exchange? One can say that had we not found money or pulling with a gentile, we would not have established it as exchange. Alternatively, one can say that when it says “a gentile with one,” it is not speaking of exchange, which is the same for a gentile and for a Jew, but of a new acquisition, such as money or pulling.
tosafot:b2.1: By Torah law money acquires: Rashi explained that it is written of consecrated property, “Then he shall give the money and it shall be assured to him,” and an ordinary person is derived from consecrated property. And if you say: according to Reish Lakish, who says pulling is explicit in the Torah, let us derive that money acquires with an ordinary person as with consecrated property, and that pulling too acquires with consecrated property as with an ordinary person? The Rav, Rabbi Yehuda bar Natan, answered that pulling does not apply to consecrated property, for wherever it is, it is in the treasury of the Merciful One. That is why money fits consecrated property more than an ordinary person: for with an ordinary person, where pulling is possible, there should be no other acquisition. And it seems to the Ri that he derives it well from the verse: we expound “of your counterpart’s hand” by pulling, so from the hand of a gentile with money; and from the fact that a gentile [acquires] with one, a Jew too [acquires] with one, for the two are learned from each other. For one cannot say that the verse speaks only to say that a gentile [acquires] with either this or that, and likewise a Jew, for if so they would be the same. And even if you were to say that exchange acquires with a Jew and not with a gentile, unlike what I explained above, one can say that the verse speaks only of the usual and common acquisitions, such as money and pulling, and with these a Jew and a gentile are learned from each other. And [my] teacher further explains the reason of Rabbi Yoḥanan, that money acquires, from the verse itself, “or buy of your counterpart’s hand,” for an unspecified acquisition in Scripture is with money, as it is written, “Fields shall be bought for money” (Jeremiah 32:44), and it is written, “From the money of his purchase” (Leviticus 25:51).
tosafot:b6.1: According to the one who says robbing a Canaanite is permitted: Rashi explained that it is a dispute in HaGozel Batra (Bava Kamma 113b). But the whole discussion there shows that it is forbidden, and they disagree about withholding his loan. However, in chapter Arba Mitot (Sanhedrin 57a) it is taught: robbery, theft, and likewise a beautiful captive woman, a Jew with a Canaanite is permitted. And in chapter HaMekabel (Bava Metzia 111b) too it says: one [verse] to permit robbing a Canaanite and one to permit withholding his wages, regarding “your fellow” and “your brother.” And if you say: how is robbing a Canaanite permitted? Isn’t it written, “And he shall reckon with his purchaser” (Leviticus 25:50), which speaks of a Canaanite who is under your authority, for if he is not under his authority, who would obey, [reckoning] according to the years [remaining] until the Jubilee? One can say: where there is desecration of God’s name it is certainly forbidden, and where it is permitted is where he has a way to evade it, and he robbed him by a pretext or in various such ways.
tosafot:b8.1: And if you say money acquires, why do I need pulling: This is puzzling, for in the last chapter of Avoda Zara (71b) it brings this baraita to infer the opposite from the first clause, saying: and if you say pulling acquires with a gentile, why should he return it? And the Ri says that the questioner holds, both here and there, that with a Canaanite we require both pulling and money, and now, both here and there, the first clause and the latter clause work out well for him.
tosafot:b8.2: This is what it means: even though he gave money, if he pulled, yes; if he did not pull, no: And if you say: but there is [the curse] “He Who exacted payment” [for one who retracts after paying]? One can say: [this is] where he accepted upon himself to be judged by Jewish law, and “He Who exacted payment” is not [part of] the law. Alternatively, as Rabbeinu Tam explains in chapter HaZahav (Bava Metzia 47b), “He Who exacted payment” is needed regarding a rise or fall in price, but not where he would lose entirely. And even though just below [Ravina] explains [it as] mere words, [where] if they involved a breach of faith he would be forbidden [to retract], because it would look like idol worship in the possession of a Jew, Abaye is not concerned about the appearance of idol worship in the possession of a Jew. Moreover, here it does not appear so at all, since there is no “He Who exacted payment,” as I explained, and there is also no greater breach of faith with a gentile than with a Jew.
tosafot:b11.1: Since he gave the dinars, he should have inspected and then pulled: Even though with other mistaken transactions we do not say this, one who buys broken vessels from a gentile is different, for he should have been more mindful that perhaps there is idol worship among them.
tosafot:b12.1: In brief: Rabbeinu Tam usually rules like Rabbi Yoḥanan that by Torah law money acquires, since Rava rules in HaḤoletz (Yevamot 36a) that the halakha follows Rabbi Yoḥanan against Reish Lakish everywhere except three cases. This is difficult from here: Rav Ashi, later than Rava, says pulling does not acquire with a gentile, which implies he expounds “your counterpart” by pulling and a gentile with money, as Reish Lakish does. Answer: Rav Ashi retracted in favor of Ameimar, as the last chapter of Avoda Zara (71a) shows: Ameimar’s proof that pulling acquires with a gentile from the Persians, who send gifts to each other and do not retract, is discussed by Ravina and Rav Ashi and accepted. And when Ravina objects there to Rav Ashi from Rabbi Yoḥanan’s ruling about a descendant of Noah, Rav Ashi does not answer that Rabbi Yoḥanan follows his own view that money acquires while he himself follows Reish Lakish; so even at first Rav Ashi held like Rabbi Yoḥanan, reading money for both a Jew and a gentile and taking “your counterpart” to teach exploitation, per the view that robbing a gentile is forbidden. As for HaZahav (Bava Metzia 48a), “the verse and the mishna support Reish Lakish”: that is only at first glance; the verse can be read with Rabbi Yoḥanan, who would set the mishna’s bath attendant as a gentile and its barber as a Jew. And if you say Reish Lakish could equally set the bath attendant as a gentile: Rabbeinu Tam answers that “bath attendant” implies a Jew, like “his fellow” in that mishna, and only a bath attendant lacks no pulling (“here is the bathhouse before you, enter and bathe”). Rava did not say “the verse and the mishna support Reish Lakish” because he rules with him, for Rava himself rules with Rabbi Yoḥanan except in three cases. Nor can one say a supporting baraita makes the difference, since one of the three is already a case where a baraita supports Reish Lakish, and Ḥullin (77a), on sinews that will later harden, implies “three and no more”; Sanhedrin (15a) and Avoda Zara (6b), where baraitot support Reish Lakish, are explained otherwise. Yet the proof from Rava can be rejected: here Reish Lakish speaks in the name of Rabbi Oshaya, and Rava does not rule against Reish Lakish where he speaks in his teachers’ name, as in Ḥullin (29b), where Reish Lakish speaks for Levi the Elder and Rava follows him in Pesaḥim (63a) and Zevaḥim (30a). The report “Rava said that Rav Huna said: sell it to me for these [coins], he has acquired” should read Rabba, for Rava never saw Rav Huna: he was born the day Rav Yehuda died (Kiddushin 72b), Rav Huna died before Rav Yehuda (Mo’ed Katan 17a), and Rav Huna was senior even to Shmuel (Gittin 5a). A further proof that the halakha follows Rabbi Yoḥanan: “And so said Rav Naḥman: by Torah law money acquires,” and we follow Rav Naḥman in monetary law. Kiddushin (14b), “a gentile, whose entire acquisition is by money,” refers only to a Hebrew slave. The answer in Avoda Zara (63a) about a gentile prostitute, where pulling is not lacking, follows Reish Lakish; the other answer there, a Jewish prostitute standing in her own courtyard, fits Rabbi Yoḥanan too. Alternatively, that answer is Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak’s, who holds like Reish Lakish, and not Rav Ḥisda’s as the books read, since Rav Ḥisda says in HaZahav (Bava Metzia 47b) that the Sages instituted pulling for purchasers, i.e., like Rabbi Yoḥanan; though this too can be rejected, since he could hold like Rabbi Yoḥanan and still read “to your counterpart” as teaching exploitation. tosafot:b13.1: And the first clause means this: if he did not give money, etc.: meaning, and also if he did not pull, he may retract.
tosafot:b14.1: And this applies to a Jew from a Jew, etc.: This is puzzling: [the case] similar to the first clause, a Jew [buying] from a gentile where he loses everything, as here, where he loses the value of the idol: is there a breach of faith in such a case even between a Jew and a Jew? One can say that this is what it means: with a Jew [buying] from a gentile, if words involved a breach of faith, it would look like the value of idol worship in the possession of a Jew, [for] even though it is a mistaken transaction, he would have to uphold the sale so that there be no breach of faith.
gershom:a1.1: Rav Sheshet says: what [does] “and redeeming a firstborn donkey immediately” [mean]? To say that if he redeemed it before thirty [days], he does not transgress over it, even though he redeemed it not at the time of its mitzva.
gershom:a2.1: What, does “its mitzva is throughout thirty” not mean that it is a mitzva to keep it for all thirty [days] before he redeems it? Evidently, if he redeemed it earlier, he transgresses over it.
gershom:a3.1: No: it means it is a mitzva to redeem it throughout thirty [days], for within thirty, up to thirty, is the time of its redemption, and if he did not redeem it by thirty,
gershom:a4.1: he transgresses over it from then on. If so: since you establish that it is a mitzva to redeem it throughout thirty [days], [then] where it teaches “from then on (from thirty onward) either he redeems it or breaks its neck,” [it should have said] “from then on either he breaks its neck or he transgresses over it,” since the time of its redemption has already passed. [A note in the printed edition: Rabbeinu Gershom’s text of the Gemara reads “If so, from then on either he breaks its neck or he transgresses over it,” where ours reads “either he redeems it or he transgresses,” and he explains that according to Rav Sheshet there is no remedy by redemption at all after thirty days.] Rather, since it teaches “either he redeems it or breaks its neck,” learn from this that it says “either he redeems it” because from then on is the time of its redemption. Evidently it is a mitzva to keep it, and Rav Sheshet’s explanation, “to say that he does not transgress over it,” does not hold; and by your reasoning, [the baraitot] contradict each other.
gershom:a5.1: Rather, Rava says: it is not difficult. This which teaches “and with redemption of the son and a firstborn donkey, [not] less than thirty” is Rabbi Eliezer, who compares the firstborn of a non-kosher animal to the firstborn of a person, as it is written, “But you shall surely redeem,” etc. (Numbers 18:15); and this which teaches “and redeeming a firstborn donkey immediately” is the Rabbis, who do not compare.
gershom:a6.1: For the sake of the mitzva: to build up his brother’s house.
gershom:a7.1: Initially: when people were upright. And now, that they do not intend it for the sake of the mitzva, but for the sake of intercourse.
gershom:a8.1: They said the mitzva of ḥalitza takes precedence: for since he does not have intercourse for the sake of the mitzva, it is as though he encounters a forbidden relation.
gershom:a9.1: The mitzva of redeeming a non-kosher animal by the owner takes precedence over redemption by anyone else, because the owners add a fifth when they redeem it, while anyone else who redeems it does not add a fifth, as it is written: “And if it is of a non-kosher animal, then he shall redeem it according to your valuation and shall add a fifth part of it to it; and if it is not redeemed” by the owner, “it shall be sold according to your valuation” to anyone.
gershom:a11.1: They were exempted only from redemption of the son and the firstborn donkey: as it says in the previous chapter, “But you shall surely redeem the firstborn of man, and the firstborn of the non-kosher animal”: whoever is [subject] to the firstborn of man is [subject] to the firstborn of a non-kosher animal, etc. Evidently they were exempted only from these two laws.
gershom:a12.1: Inherent sanctity: for it cannot be redeemed.
gershom:a13.1: Because it is dear to him, in accordance with Rabbi Ḥanina, who said [above]: for they assisted Israel, etc.
gershom:a14.1: Because its matters are few: for it is discussed only in the first chapter, but the whole tractate discusses the firstborn of a kosher animal.
gershom:a15.1: According to their laws: that is, any trade where a gentile’s hand is in the middle must follow his law; we follow their laws, and in their laws money acquires.
gershom:a16.1: If we say according to the laws of his person: of a gentile, who is acquired by a Jew with money, since the verse compared him to an ancestral possession, as it is written, “And you may make them an inheritance,” etc.: just as an ancestral possession is acquired with money, a document and taking possession, so too a Canaanite slave.
gershom:a17.1: And furthermore, “from the money of his purchase” implies [acquisition] with money both [by] a Jew from a gentile and [by] a gentile from a Jew.
gershom:a18.1: His property, his animal, all the more so: however, we do not accept this, [for] a Jew from a Jew will prove it: his person one acquires with money, as we said, “from the money of his purchase,” and his property by pulling.
gershom:a19.1: “Of your counterpart’s hand”: it is by pulling, for it is written “hand,” a thing given from hand to hand. From the hand of a gentile, with money.
gershom:a20.1: And say that this is why the verse comes: from the hand of your counterpart he acquires; from the hand of a gentile, not at all, for if the gentile wishes to retract, he can retract. This cannot be said, for if he acquires his person with money, all the more so his property.
gershom:b1.1: And say: from the hand of your counterpart by pulling alone; from the hand of a gentile, not until there are both, money and pulling.
gershom:b2.1: Similar to your counterpart: just as your counterpart with one, by pulling and not with money, so a gentile with one, with money and not by pulling. And as we said: to a gentile not at all, that he does not acquire from a Jew either by pulling or with money.
gershom:b3.1: They said: is it not an a fortiori inference? [If] he acquires the person of a Jew with money, all the more so his property, his animal. [The printed edition notes that this belongs to amud a.]
gershom:b4.1: And according to Ameimar, who says in Bava Metzia that pulling acquires with a gentile: this works out well if he holds like Rabbi Yoḥanan, who says that by Torah law money acquires, a Jew from a Jew, and not pulling. He resolves it thus: to your counterpart with money, and to a gentile by pulling. That is why it needed to write “to your counterpart”: your counterpart with money, and not a gentile; and he reverses the teaching of Rabbi Yitzḥak [bar Naḥmani]. But if he holds like Reish Lakish, etc., then what does “to your counterpart” come to exclude, since both are by pulling?
gershom:b5.1: And one to exclude consecrated property: so that you should not say the power of an ordinary person should not be greater than consecrated property; it teaches us “your counterpart,” and not consecrated property.
gershom:b6.1: His robbery is forbidden: of a gentile.
gershom:b7.1: If he holds like the one who says his robbery is permitted, and “to your counterpart” is not needed for exploitation, perforce Ameimar holds like Rabbi Yoḥanan, who says by Torah law money acquires; therefore “to your counterpart” is needed: to your counterpart with money, and to a gentile by pulling.
gershom:b9.1: He takes the benefit to the Dead Sea: for now they are his, and it is forbidden to keep it in his possession, and forbidden for him to sell it.
gershom:b10.1: If so, the first clause is difficult: for why should he return it? He pulled, and he should have to take it to the Dead Sea.
gershom:b11.1: For there is a mistaken transaction: for he did not know that there was idol worship among them.
gershom:b12.1: The first clause and the latter clause are a mistaken transaction: and pulling acquires, since he accepted to be judged by Jewish law.
gershom:b13.1: And Abaye would say to you: really, it is as I said: the first clause involves a mistaken transaction, for even though he pulled, since he had not yet given the dinars, he did not check whether there was idol worship among them or not; therefore he returns it.
gershom:b14.1: And the latter clause is not a mistaken transaction: for since he gave the dinars and then pulled, he should have inspected; [and since he did not inspect,] he waived [his claim], and it is not a mistaken transaction.
gershom:b15.1: What is “returns”? But he did not pull anything.
gershom:b16.1: He returns on his words: [retracting] from the terms of the transfer. [The words that follow, “And once redeemed, they are obligated in the firstborn and in the gifts, the foreleg, the jaw and the maw, since a blemish preceded the consecration, and once redeemed they are like non-sacred animals,” gloss the mishna that opens 14a.]
